plan.contextChunk: This figure consists of one large unit circle annotated with the standard special angles and the coordinates of their terminal points. A heavy black circle is centered on thin horizontal and vertical axes, and sixteen straight radii run from the center out to filled dots placed every 30 or 45 degrees around the circumference. Each dot carries an external label in two colors: the angle written in degrees and then in radians in red, followed by the point's (x, y) coordinates in black. Reading counterclockwise from the right, the labels begin 0 degrees, 0, (1, 0), with 360 degrees, 2pi, (1, 0) printed directly beneath it, then 30 degrees, pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, 1/2); 45 degrees, pi/4, (sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2); 60 degrees, pi/3, (1/2, sqrt(3)/2); and 90 degrees, pi/2, (0, 1) at the top. The second quadrant continues with 120, 135, and 150 degrees and closes at 180 degrees, pi, (-1, 0); the third runs 210, 225, and 240 degrees to 270 degrees, 3pi/2, (0, -1); and the fourth returns through 300 and 315 degrees to 330 degrees, 11pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, -1/2). The symmetric placement is the point of the layout, since the same three magnitudes 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, and sqrt(3)/2 recur in every quadrant with only their signs changing. Gathering all the major angles on one circle lets values outside the first quadrant be recovered by reflection rather than recomputed.

interactionPlan.concept: The unit circle collects every special angle so that any quadrant's terminal point is found by reflecting the first-quadrant values (the same magnitudes 1/2, √2/2, √3/2 with sign changes), and each point's coordinates are exactly (cos θ, sin θ).
elements: thin horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis through the center with arrowheads
heavy black unit circle centered at the origin
sixteen radii from the center to the circumference at every 30° and 45° increment
sixteen filled black terminal-point dots on the circle
red angle labels at each dot giving degrees then radians (e.g. 30°, π/6; 90°, π/2; 180°, π; 270°, 3π/2; 360°, 2π)
black coordinate labels at each dot giving the (x, y) terminal point (e.g. (√3/2, 1/2), (√2/2, √2/2), (1/2, √3/2), (0,1), (-1,0), etc.)
horizontal projection segment from a clicked point to the y-axis (the cos θ component)
vertical projection segment from a clicked point to the x-axis (the sin θ component)
small right-angle marker where the projections meet the axes
highlight outline rings drawn on the symmetric terminal points sharing the hovered point's reference angle

interactions.label: Label set
interactions.teaches: Degrees, radians, and the (x, y) coordinate triple are three names for the very same fixed terminal point — switching sets declutters the circle without moving any dot

Pointing at one dot brightens its label and outlines the dots with the same reference angle in the other quadrants, exposing that every quadrant reuses the same three magnitudes (1/2, √2/2, √3/2) with only the signs flipped by reflection
Clicking a ray drops perpendicular projections to both axes, rebuilding the terminal point as (cos θ, sin θ) — the x-projection is the cosine and the y-projection is the sine of that angle

demo_steps.title: One circle, all special angles
demo_steps.narration: The full label set shows every 30° and 45° terminal point at once: red degree+radian names and black coordinates around a single unit circle.

demo_steps.narration: Hover the 30° point (√3/2, 1/2): the 150°, 210°, and 330° dots light up too, because they all share the 30° reference angle and differ only in the signs of the same √3/2 and 1/2 magnitudes.

demo_steps.title: Coordinates are cosine and sine
demo_steps.narration: Click the 60° ray: a horizontal segment reaches the x-axis at 1/2 and a vertical one reaches the y-axis at √3/2, showing the point is exactly (cos 60°, sin 60°).

demo_steps.title: Three names, one point
demo_steps.narration: Toggle the label set between angle and coordinate views — the dots never move, confirming that 60°, π/3, and (1/2, √3/2) all describe the identical terminal point.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Every special-angle coordinate on the unit circle is just (cos θ, sin θ), and the whole table collapses to three magnitudes (1/2, √2/2, √3/2) whose signs are set by the quadrant via reflection.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Center the heavy black circle on thin crossing axes with arrowheads at all four ends. Place 16 filled dots at 0,30,45,60,90,...,330 degrees with thin radii to each. Angle text (degrees then radians, e.g. '90°, π/2') in red just outside each dot; the coordinate pair in black beside it, typeset with fraction bars and √ symbols. Keep the symmetric layout exact so reflection is visually obvious. On hover, draw a colored outline ring on the three other dots sharing the reference angle and brighten the hovered label. On click, draw a dashed horizontal segment from the point to the y-axis and a dashed vertical segment to the x-axis in two distinct colors, with a small right-angle square at the foot, and tag them cos θ and sin θ. The label toggle hides/shows the red angle text versus the black coordinate text (or both).

authoredContext:
Now that we have learned how to find the cosine and sine values for special angles in the first quadrant, we can use symmetry and reference angles to fill in cosine and sine values for the rest of the special angles on the unit circle. They are shown in the figure. Take time to learn the (x,y) coordinates of all of the major angles in the first quadrant.

Special angles and coordinates of corresponding points on the unit circle

Graph of unit circle with angles in degrees, angles in radians, and points along the circle inscribed.
